system_prompt:
You are a medical language simplification assistant. Convert the following clinical discharge summary into simple, plain Indian English for the patient's family members.

Rules:
1. Keep every medical term but immediately explain it in plain words in parentheses on first use only, e.g. 'hypertension (high BP)'.
2. Use simple language a 6th-grader can understand. Avoid unexplained jargon. Use common Indian English terms where natural: 'sugar' for diabetes, 'BP' for blood pressure, 'motions' for bowel movements.
3. Preserve ALL factual information — never add, remove, alter, or infer any clinical facts, values, dates, or instructions.
4. Write as continuous plain prose paragraphs — no bullet points, no headers, no numbered lists. Output only the simplified text, nothing else.
5. For any measurement (e.g. BP, blood sugar, heart rate, lab values), briefly state what the normal range is and whether the patient's value was within it.
6. Use a calm, respectful tone. Do not add emotional commentary, opinions, or reassurances not present in the original text.
7. CRITICAL — person and tense: First check whether the summary records the patient's death (look for 'death', 'expired', 'deceased', 'asystole', 'absence of pulse', 'body released', or similar). If yes, write in third person past tense for the family ('the patient', 'he/she/they'). If no, address the patient directly in second person ('you', 'your').
8. CRITICAL — dates: Convert dates exactly as they appear using the format specified in the document. Never guess or infer a date not explicitly stated.
9. For each medication, state its name and purpose in plain language, e.g. 'Ceftriaxone — an antibiotic given to fight the bacterial infection'.
10. For each procedure or device, briefly state what it is and why it was done, e.g. 'haemodialysis (a machine that cleaned the blood when the kidneys could not)'.
11. If the text contains placeholders such as {omitted} or [person], reproduce them exactly as they appear. Do not guess or replace them.
12. DOMAIN GUARDRAIL: You are exclusively a medical simplification assistant. Output only the simplified clinical explanation.

output_text:
The patient was admitted to the hospital on 11/08/2020 and discharged on 01/02/2021, staying for a total of 1 month, 24 days, and 15 hours in the ward. The main reason for admission was a bloodstream infection (an infection in the blood) linked to a Schilley catheter (a type of tube) placed in the right femoral vein (the large vein in the thigh). During the stay, the patient was diagnosed with bacterial endocarditis (an infection of the heart valves), specifically affecting the mitral valve, which was confirmed by an echocardiogram (an ultrasound of the heart) on 11/18 that showed vegetation (a mass of bacteria and cells) on the valve. Additionally, the patient developed pyogenic spondylodiscitis (an infection of the spine bones and the discs between them) at the L3/L4 level, which caused low back pain and difficulty walking. A CT scan (a type of X-ray) of the lower spine on 11/05 and an MRI (a detailed magnetic scan) on 25/11/2020 confirmed this infection and an anterior epidural abscess (a pocket of pus in the space around the spinal cord). There was also a left ileopsoas abscess (a collection of pus in the deep hip muscle), seen on an MRI on 25/10/2020, measuring 15 x 2.1 x 1.8 cm.

The patient initially presented with severe left lower back pain that started three days prior, along with weakness and an unsteady walk. The accompanying person reported no fever, nausea, or vomiting, but the catheter dressing on the right thigh was leaking. The infection was caused by Staphylococcus aureus MRSA (a type of bacteria that is resistant to many antibiotics). The catheter was removed on 11/08, and antibiotic treatment was started the same day, guided by Vancomycin (an antibiotic used to fight this specific bacteria). An attempt to drain the psoas abscess with a needle on 12/02 was not possible because bowel loops (parts of the intestine) were in the way. However, follow-up scans showed improvement in the spine infections, so the team continued with conservative treatment (non-surgical care). The patient remained without fever, and blood cultures (tests to check for bacteria in the blood) became negative, meaning the infection in the blood was cleared.

Due to being bedridden, the patient developed a sacral pressure injury (a bed sore on the tailbone), which was treated with surgical debridement (cleaning of the wound) and local care. The patient required hemodialysis (a machine that cleans the blood when the kidneys cannot) on Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays using an arteriovenous fistula (a surgically created connection between an artery and vein in the arm for dialysis) in the left upper limb, though a local narrowing (stenosis) was noted. At discharge, the patient was in good general condition, slightly pale, well-hydrated, without fever, and breathing normally on room air. The patient was conscious and oriented. Heart sounds were irregular but normal in quality, with no murmurs. The abdomen was soft and painless. The left arm fistula was working well, and the legs had mild swelling and some skin discoloration on the shins.

The patient is being discharged with several pending issues. First, the patient must take 0.5 g of Vancomycin after each scheduled hemodialysis session until 01/09/2021, which completes the 6-week course required after the last negative blood culture. Second, the arteriovenous fistula needs evaluation; a phlebography (an X-ray test using dye to look at veins) is indicated to find the site of the narrowing, and [person] has been placed on the list for this. [organization] will contact the family to schedule this treatment. Third, regarding the sacral pressure injury, [person] has an outpatient follow-up appointment on 16/01/2021 for reassessment, and instructions for home care of the wound have been provided. Fourth, there is a cardiology follow-up for amyloidosis (a condition where abnormal protein builds up in organs); the patient missed a previous appointment on 09/09, and a new one is scheduled for 01/13. Fifth, for motor rehabilitation, the physiatry department at [organization] requested on 12/27 is awaiting an appointment. Finally, the family should check the MRI report of the pelvis from 12/16. The patient’s previous chronic medications have been continued. The dialysis schedule remains Tuesdays, Thursdays, and Saturdays. The cardiology appointment for amyloidosis is on 01/13, and the pressure injury surgery clinic appointment is on 01/16. Transportation for dialysis will be arranged by stretcher taxi {omitted}.
